category_title: Ninth-grade students labeled as struggling readers who engage through inquiry-based disciplinary literacy
minimal_context: The student is listening to a 10-minute lecture on imperialism and the U.S. annexation of Hawai'i while the 'Petition Against Annexation' is displayed on the document camera.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's begin our 10-minute lecture on imperialism and the U.S. annexation of Hawai'i. I have the 1897 'Petition Against Annexation' on the document camera, so please take notes as I talk.

STUDENT: (Coughs and pulls her gray sweatshirt tighter, staring blankly at the document camera without picking up her pencil.)

TUTOR: Please make sure you are following along with the lecture.

STUDENT: (Leans back in her chair, appearing tired, and still does not take any notes.)

TUTOR: It is important to get this information down.

STUDENT: (Coughs again and rests her head on her hand, completely unengaged with the lecture and leaving her paper blank.)

options.A: Integrate historical films into the teaching of imperialism to support literacy learning and avoid presenting the subject material purely as abstract facts.
options.B: Implement relatively tight timelines for the lecture and note-taking activities during the multiday lessons on imperialism and annexation.
options.C: Purposefully select historical texts and primary sources that are written by and/or feature people of color for the lessons on imperialism and annexation.
options.D: Build a classroom community where students feel safe taking risks, diligently protecting them by ensuring no answer is ever treated as stupid during historical inquiry.
